How "Teen People" Magazine Encourages Drug Abuse By Lying to Kids About Marijuana

Teen People Magazine April 1998

Page: 120

By Gail Hoch O’Connor

Page: 120

By Gail Hoch O’Connor

HEALTHTALK: MJ MYTHS.

You’re Sure That Pot’s Illegal, But How Much Do You Really Know About It?

Here’s A Look At What’s Fact And What’s Fiction

Myth #1: "Pot is not addictive- I can stop whenever I want." Marijuana IS an addictive drug. The hazy, almost dreamlike state some people achieve from smoking pot can be very seductive, especially if you’re stressed or depressed." says Martha Gagne, director of the American Council for Drug Education. "Suddenly, when you want to escape your problems or even to feel good about yourself, you need that high." That’s called psychological addiction. It’s in your head. (Ed. note: First, anything can be "psychologically" addictive, including marijuana, and the Internet. This tells kids nothing, but is misleading by making it appear to be something unique to chemicals.)

But marijuana may also be physically addictive. After you haven’t smoked for a while, you may experience such withdrawal symptoms as sweating, jitteriness and nausea. (Ed. note: This is utter non-sense. There is no such abstinence syndrome for marijuana. There is no data even in the most extreme prohibitionist propaganda that supports this. Telling kids this is very counterproductive.)

One recent study has shown that pot has the same addictive effect on the brain as heroin. (Ed. note: No, what this study showed was that the pleasure derived from using cannabis stimulated the same part of the brain as heroin and alcohol, etc. This is not at all the same thing as equating the addictive potential of heroin and marijuana. Telling kids this is also the same as telling them that heroin is no more addictive than marijuana. Is this really what Teen People wants teen people to believe?) See

Myth #2: "It won’t do any serious damage to my body." In guys, heavy, chronic pot smoking can delay the onset of puberty, decrease sperm count and make sperm abnormal. In girls, such marijuana use can mess with menstrual cycles and decrease fertility. It may also raise levels of testostorone (the male hormone), which pumps up facial and body hair growth and causes acne. Not pretty. (Ed. note: this is all non-sense, but pre-teens, pubescent children should certainly not be "heavy, chronic" smokers unless they have a serious medical condition. So this is irrelevant to most teens.) Another uncool fact: When you are stoned, your responses are slower and you aren’t able to think as clearlly, which increases your risk of doing something you will really regret- like not using a condom during sex, or driving a car when your reflexes are totally shot. (Ed. note: Congratulations! This is close enough to being accurate.)

Myth #3: "I can just stick with pot, I don’t have to get into any other drugs." Even if you swear you’ll never try cocaine or heroin, as a pot smoker you may end up doing a hard-core drug without even realizing it. How? Simply, there’s no way to tell if the joint, blunt or bong being passed your way contains pot that’s been laced with something else- like cocaine, crack, heroin or acid. So you might sample another dangerous drug and become physically addicted to it. (Ed. note: Good grief! This is actually an argument against marijuana prohibition, but not a very good one. The chances of someone lacing marijuana with something else are very small, but no one becomes addicted by sampling an unknown substance. But no one should smoke with people that they don’t know to be cool. They could be narks or some other dangerous types.)

Myth #4: "If I get caught, I’ll only be in serious trouble with my parents." Forget how your folks would react: If you get busted for using marijuana, they just might be visiting you in jail. Depending on the state you live in, you risk landing yourself a sentence ranging from probation to something more severe, like a stretch of time at a residential drug-treatment center or a juvenile detention center.

(Ed. note: Yes, thanks to this kind of non-sense, you could be in very serious trouble with the law, if you get caught. You should be in serious trouble with your family, if you are risking bringing financial ruin on them just to get high. This is the most compelling reason for anyone, but especially kids, not to smoke. However, this is an argument against the cruel laws of marijuana prohibition, not against marijuana.)

Pot by the Numbers:

5-the number of cigs you would have to smoke to do the kind of damage to your lungs that smoking one joint does.

(Ed. note: No, this is simply wrong. This is based on some studies that show that marijuana cigarettes, being more loosely rolled give up more particulate and tar than tobacco cigarettes. It also relates to the unnecessary practice of holding marijuana smoke in the lungs. However, recent studies have also shown that machine tests of tobacco smoke may been understating the amount of tar consumed.

In any case, there have been no known cases of lung cancer attributable solely to marijuana. Moreover, the 1997 Kaiser Permanente long-term study of 65,000 marijuana smokers found that marijuana smokers had only a slightly higher instance of respiratory problems than did non-smokers.

Another 1997 study published by the Australian government found that 268 regular marijuana smokers over a nineteen year period had a lower rate of emphysema and asthma than did the general population. Teens should not be heavy marijuana smokers, but telling them that it is five times worse than tobacco is to encourage the addiction that kills more Americans than all the others combined.)

30- The approximate percentage of teens who have used pot at least once in the past year. That’s just 3 out of 10, so forget using "peer pressure" as an excuse to light up. (Ed. note: Excellent advice, but totally irrelevant. Kids go with their own peers, not an average of all teens from 13 to 19.)

20- some marijuana is 20 times more potent now than it was a few decades ago. (Newer,stronger strains are being cultivated), so it’s MORE HARMFUL to your body and brain than ever before.

(Ed. note: Where do they get these numbers? There is absolutely no data to support this. The US government data shows that the average potency has been around 3% for twenty years. If average marijuana potency is only 3% today, Teen People’s statement would mean that decades ago marijuana had only half as much THC as industrial hemp can have today. Moreover, there is no data to support the notion that higher THC levels make marijuana more harmful.)

6- The number of months in jail actor Robert Downey Jr.- who told Diane Sawyer on PrimeTime Live that he was ADDICTED TO POT at age eight- is serving for drug-related offenses.

(If Mr. Downey was "addicted to pot" at age eight, he certainly must have had a lot of other problems. No one should be in jail for simply having a "drug problem.")

need more info???

If you want to know more about marijuana or other drugs, contact:

America Council for Drug Education Helpline: 800-DRUGHELP; www.acde.org

The National Clearinghouse for Alcohol and Drug Information: 800-729-6686 or 301-468-2600; www.health.org

Pot Almost Ruined My Life- Rhianne Alexoff, 17, is a recovering pot abuser and drug addict. She checked into Phoenix Academy, a residential drug-treatment facility in the San Diego area, about a year ago to get clean.

This is her story:

The first time I used pot I was 12. I was with a crown of older kids and someone passed me a joint. I didn’t want to seem like a little kid, so I smoked it- and then I started hanging out with that crowd. When it was time for me to start high school, I only stayed a week. My mother begged me not to drop out, but I didn’t listen. I got my GED at 16, but I wasn’t done partying. I even sold drugs on the side. My mom was worried about me, and she asked me to come to Phoenix Academy. When I first got here I thought pot was okay because it’s a plant- it’s natural. Now I know that anything that alters your mind is a drug. I plan on going to college soon. Whatever I do, I definitely don’t plan on doing drugs."

(Ed. note: Good for her. If she had had accurate credible information marijuana, maybe she wouldn’t have smoked at twelve. She also would not have thought that just because they had lied to her about marijuana, they had lied about everything else.

When we tell children non-sense like this article we make drug abuse more – not less – likely. And will teens really be convinced by "anecdotal evidence" when they see others smoke marijuana and do well in school.

Nowhere in this article is the key point that individuals vary greatly. Most kids do not have problems with marijuana, but this is no guarantee that you won’t. That is a very important message that simply cannot be taught in the world of reefer madness which places emphasis on the "dangers" of marijuana and not on individual vulnerabilities.

The sources for data on this include the National Institute on Drug Abuse and Marijuana Myths; Marijuana Facts. This book has detailed citations for all of its data, unlike this article.)
